quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE TARGET CONSONANT PHONEME IN THE WORD
quests.hint: Try producing "half" yourself. To make /f/, you rest your top teeth lightly on your bottom lip and blow with no voice — quite different from /v/, which needs you to rest your top teeth lightly on your bottom lip and blow with your voice on.
quests.explanation: Once you isolate the consonant in "half", it's clearly /f/ — produced by resting your top teeth lightly on your bottom lip and blowing with no voice. Words with /v/ instead, like "van", require resting your top teeth lightly on your bottom lip and blowing with your voice on.
quests.mouthPosition: Rest your top teeth lightly on your bottom lip and blow with no voice.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE TARGET CONSONANT PHONEME IN THE WORD
quests.hint: Here's the key contrast in "proof": /f/ is made by resting your top teeth lightly on your bottom lip and blowing with no voice, and /v/ is made by resting your top teeth lightly on your bottom lip and blowing with your voice on. Which description fits what you hear?
quests.explanation: /f/ is the sound in "proof", formed by resting your top teeth lightly on your bottom lip and blowing with no voice. Learners often mix this up with /v/, a voiced labiodental fricative made by resting your top teeth lightly on your bottom lip and blowing with your voice on, but the mouth is doing something different each time.
quests.mouthPosition: To produce this sound, rest your top teeth lightly on your bottom lip and blow with no voice.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE TARGET CONSONANT PHONEME IN THE WORD
quests.hint: Don't let the spelling of "time" guide you — isolate the exact consonant sound and test it against both options.
quests.explanation: This is /t/, not /d/: in "time", you tap your tongue tip on the ridge behind your top teeth with no voice. The distractor would instead need tapping your tongue tip on the ridge behind your top teeth with your voice on, which changes the sound completely.
quests.mouthPosition: Feel it in the mouth: tap your tongue tip on the ridge behind your top teeth with no voice.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE TARGET CONSONANT PHONEME IN THE WORD
quests.hint: For /θ/, the trick is to place your tongue tip lightly behind your top teeth and blow with no voice — like the start of "think". Check whether "fifth" really does that.
quests.explanation: "fifth" is built on /θ/ — placing your tongue tip lightly behind your top teeth and blowing with no voice is how it's made. That's a voiceless dental fricative, easy to tell apart from the voiceless alveolar fricative /s/ once you know both feel different in the mouth.
quests.mouthPosition: Place your tongue tip lightly behind your top teeth and blow with no voice.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE TARGET CONSONANT PHONEME IN THE WORD
quests.hint: "game" needs careful listening. A voiced velar plosive like /g/ can sound close to a voiceless velar plosive like /k/ if you're not paying attention to exactly what your mouth is doing.
quests.explanation: "game" features /g/ rather than /k/. /g/ comes from raising the back of your tongue to the soft palate with your voice on, which is why it sounds distinct from the voiceless velar plosive /k/ used in words like "key".
quests.mouthPosition: To produce this sound, raise the back of your tongue to the soft palate with your voice on.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE TARGET CONSONANT PHONEME IN THE WORD
quests.hint: Whisper "think" to yourself and freeze on the target consonant. Is your mouth doing this — placing your tongue tip lightly behind your top teeth and blowing with no voice — or this — pushing a thin stream of air over your tongue tip with no voice?

The distractor /s/ would instead require you to push a thin stream of air over your tongue tip with no voice — a clearly different sound once you isolate it.
